html:
In 729, a prince, his wife, and his sons all took their own lives on the same day. Eight years later, the four brothers who had driven them to it were dead, all from the same disease, all in the same year. People began to whisper that it was a curse.

The Nara period begins in 710, when the capital moved to Heijo-kyo, and it ends in 794, when the capital moved to Heian-kyo. The capital's lifespan: just eighty-four years. And in that time, the capital kept moving house again and again.

Here's the answer first. The capital never settled down because the country was hit by three shocks, over and over: feuds between powerful families, epidemics and disasters, and the problem of who would inherit the throne. Let's read the Nara period through those three shocks.

Before the Shaking: Fujiwara no Fuhito's Blueprint (710)

With its capital at Heijo-kyo, today's city of Nara, Japan began building a full-scale state run by written law. At the center of that effort was Fujiwara no Fuhito.

Fuhito's method was to marry his daughters to emperors. If a grandson became emperor, Fuhito would be the emperor's grandfather. He pulled this off across two generations, and the Fujiwara family became tightly bound to the imperial family.

Have you heard of the Habsburgs in Europe? They were the family that expanded their lands not through war, but through marriage. Fuhito's thinking was close to that. He took power not with the sword, but with the wedding.

Shock One: Family Feuds (The Nagaya Incident, 729)

But once Fuhito died, his blueprint started to shake almost at once.

The man who stepped into the center of government was Prince Nagaya, a member of the imperial family. Meanwhile, Fuhito's four sons wanted a government run not by the emperor, but by the Fujiwara family.

In 729, Prince Nagaya was accused of plotting against the state, and he took his own life. This is the Nagaya Incident. Real power passed into the hands of the four Fujiwara brothers.

But the seesaw soon tipped the other way. The next to take power was Tachibana no Moroe, who came from the imperial family. A young Fujiwara, Fujiwara no Hirotsugu, resented this. He was sent away to Kyushu, and in 740, he raised an army. This is the Rebellion of Fujiwara no Hirotsugu. It was put down quickly, but the mood in the capital turned uneasy overnight.

Shock Two: Plague, Disasters and the Great Buddha (737 to 752)

What ended the four Fujiwara brothers' rule wasn't an enemy. It was a massive epidemic in 737. All four brothers died of the disease in the same year.

From there, the fear of the people in the capital kept growing. And in the middle of Hirotsugu's rebellion, Emperor Shomu suddenly left the capital and headed east.

For the next five years, the capital wandered. Kuni-kyo, Naniwa-no-miya, Shigaraki-no-miya. The place Tachibana no Moroe backed and the place backed by the rising Fujiwara no Nakamaro didn't match, so the capital never stayed put.

To calm the fear, Emperor Shomu turned to Buddhism. In 743, he announced that he would build a gigantic statue of the Buddha.

But the people doing the actual work were ordinary people. Under that heavy burden, their anger grew, fires broke out one after another, and earthquakes kept coming. Emperor Shomu took it to mean that even heaven was angry, and in 745, he moved the capital back to Heijo-kyo. The Great Buddha was completed in 752.

This is the high point of the Nara period. That Great Buddha isn't a symbol of a wealthy nation. It's the shape of a cornered nation's prayer.

Shock Three: An Empress, a Monk and the Throne (764 to 770)

Emperor Shomu was succeeded by his daughter, Empress Koken. But the one who actually ran the government was her mother, Empress Dowager Komyo, Fuhito's daughter. The Empress Dowager relied heavily on Fujiwara no Nakamaro, and Empress Koken, without real power, handed the throne to Emperor Junnin. Emperor Junnin had been raised in Nakamaro's household.

When the Empress Dowager died, the retired Empress Koken was finally free to act. At her side was a monk named Dokyo, who had won her trust by nursing her through an illness.

Think of Rasputin, the man who worked his way into the family of Russia's last tsar. A holy man who enters the heart of the court through a sickbed. It's that same picture.

In 764, the two camps clashed in battle, and Nakamaro was defeated and killed. Emperor Junnin was exiled to Awaji Island, and the retired empress took the throne a second time, as Empress Shotoku.

Empress Shotoku tried to make Dokyo the next emperor. A monk, neither royal nor noble, on the throne. The nobles banded together and stopped it. That was in 769.

The Final Move: Leaving Nara (784 and 794)

In 770, Empress Shotoku died without naming an heir, and the nobles hurried to put Emperor Konin on the throne. Here, the imperial line switched from the bloodline of Emperor Tenmu to the bloodline of Emperor Tenji, the two brothers of the Asuka period.

Emperor Konin's son, Emperor Kanmu, thought it over. Heijo-kyo was the capital of the old bloodline. A new bloodline needs a new capital.

In 784, the capital moved to Nagaoka-kyo. But people close to the emperor died one after another, diviners blamed vengeful spirits, and the rivers flooded on top of it all. Emperor Kanmu gave up on Nagaoka-kyo too, and in 794, he moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto. And with that, the Nara period came to a close.

The Nara Period in One Line

Family feuds, epidemics and disasters, and the question of an heir. Pushed along by these three shocks, the capital kept moving, and after eighty-four years, it left Nara behind.

Here's a question for you. If you were Emperor Shomu, would you have built the Great Buddha, or spent that wealth feeding your people?

Next up: the Heian period. This time, the capital lasts about four hundred years. Let's see what changed.
